method: Blind solve from the blind files in verification/blind-u1/apush-u1-l4/ only; no question file was opened before these answers were recorded. Lesson read as a student first.
student_read_doubts: Palmares is in Brazil, a Portuguese colony, but this lesson is about Spanish America. Why is the largest Maroon example Portuguese, not Spanish?
The lesson says enslaved people kept religions 'such as voodoo' — voodoo sounds like a later Haitian religion, not something from the 1500s. Is that in period?

The repartimiento numbers: 'about one in seven men for farm work and about four percent for the mines' — two different fractions for two different drafts, but a student could read them as contradictory.
Population shares (peninsulares + criollos 1-2%, mestizos 4-5%) are given as exact-sounding numbers — do the books actually give those figures?
The first asiento details (August 1518, Laurent de Gouvenot, 4,000 people, 25,000 ducats) are very specific — need to check against the books.

apush-saq-0020.a: Epidemic disease killed enormous numbers of Native people who had no immunity to European illnesses, destroying the workforce the encomienda depended on.
apush-saq-0020.b: With the Native workforce destroyed by disease, the mines and plantations still needed workers, so Spain imported enslaved Africans under the asiento.
apush-saq-0020.c: The shift changed who was forced to work — enslaved Africans replaced Native workers — while the demand for coerced labor stayed. (From the lesson: it also made slavery lifelong and hereditary and brought large African populations whose descendants shaped colonial culture.)

apush-saq-0021.a: Sepulveda claimed Native peoples were by nature inferior and incapable of governing themselves — 'natural slaves.'
apush-saq-0021.b: By calling the wars 'just wars' fought to bring Christianity and civilized rule, his argument gave conquest a moral justification: taking land and labor was right, not theft.
apush-saq-0021.c: Sepulveda never visited the Americas, so his claims came from books and theology, not observation; he was also arguing a case to defend the conquest before the Crown, which shaped what he said. (The 'never visited' fact comes from the lesson, not the stimulus.)

apush-saq-0022.a: Bartolome de las Casas, the Dominican friar; the caption names him Bishop of Chiapa and 'defender of the Indians.'
apush-saq-0022.b: He campaigned against the abuses of the encomienda and helped push the Crown to pass the New Laws of 1542, which limited the encomienda and forbade new grants. (This comes from the lesson, not the engraving stimulus.)
apush-saq-0022.c: The engraving is 18th-century, made long after Las Casas's death, so it is an idealized imagining of how later generations remembered him, not a portrait drawn from life. (The 1791 date and 225-year gap come from the lesson.)

apush-saq-0023.a: Peninsulares, Spaniards born in Spain (or criollos, Spaniards born in the Americas).
apush-saq-0023.b: Because ancestry fixed a person's legal and social rank, the system needed a label for every mixture as Spanish, Indigenous, and African peoples mixed; it recognized finer gradations based on the specific percentage of each lineage.
apush-saq-0023.c: Your ancestry fixed your rank, which decided your access to offices, land, and legal standing — peninsulares and criollos held the offices and the land while Native peoples and Africans stood at the bottom.

apush-saq-0024.a: The New Laws declared Native peoples free subjects of the Crown, not slaves; forbade new encomienda grants; ordered existing grants to end at the holder's death; and banned enslavement of Native peoples.
apush-saq-0024.b: Las Casas's campaign denouncing Spanish cruelty pushed the Crown to act and limit the abuses. (This comes from the lesson, not the stimulus.)
apush-saq-0024.c: Colonists who depended on Native labor resisted, and the Crown backed away from enforcing the laws; enforcement was weak and the king was an ocean away. (This comes from the lesson, not the stimulus.)

apush-leq-0007.thesis: Epidemic disease was the most important cause of the shift from Native to African forced labor in Spanish America from 1542 to 1607, because it destroyed the Native workforce the encomienda depended on; the New Laws and the asiento mattered but followed from that collapse.
apush-leq-0007.outline: Context: the encomienda system and the demand for silver and plantation labor. Evidence: (1) disease killed enormous numbers of Native people with no immunity, collapsing the Native workforce; (2) the New Laws of 1542 limited the encomienda after Las Casas's campaign; (3) the first asiento (1518) and African slavery becoming lifelong and hereditary. Analysis: the causes worked together — disease created the shortage, the New Laws closed off Native labor, and the asiento supplied enslaved Africans; the demand for coerced labor never went away.

apush-leq-0008.thesis: Ancestry largely determined a person's place in Spanish colonial society from 1500 to 1607, fixing legal rank and access to offices and land, though mixing kept blurring the lines the system tried to draw.
apush-leq-0008.outline: Context: the encomienda and the mixing of peoples in the colonies. Evidence: (1) peninsulares and criollos, 1-2% of the population, held the offices and the land; (2) mestizos, mulattos, Native peoples, and Africans ranked below; (3) the two republics (republica de espanoles / republica de indios) made ancestry a legal fact. Analysis: ancestry set the rank, but mixing continued and the casta labels multiplied, showing the system constantly reasserting ranks that lived experience kept blurring.
